extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, newsletter/magazine editors, and communications managers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for producing and evaluating organizational newsletters, newspapers, magazines, and accompanying photographs/illustrations, including layout, scheduling, budgeting, story generation and evaluation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match format to publics' involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: For actively communicating publics, the publication can be a simple black-and-white newsletter with modest graphics, rather than the slick four-color magazine needed to attract low-involvement publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the production values (black-and-white vs slick four-color, modest vs elaborate graphics) based on audience involvement and problem recognition. Example: actively interested readers will accept simpler formats; low-involvement or passersby may need highly attractive materials to capture attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify expense for passive publics
rubrics_metrics.description: If your intent is to communicate with passively communicating publics, the controlled print media will work better than uncontrolled commercial media. Don’t make the mistake of believing, however, that the audience actively reads them. If you cannot demonstrate that a publication’s audience is active, make certain you can justify the expense of reaching a passive public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before committing to costly publications, demonstrate audience activity or have a cost-justification; otherwise prefer less expensive controlled-print options. Consider readership behavior (passive processing) when planning spend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use readership study to evaluate publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the communication objective is the most realistic one for a print publication, a readership study—which measures that objective—is usually the most appropriate evaluation technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate success against communication objectives via readership studies; include retention measures (e.g., signaled stopping) to determine whether audience can retain the message. Use readership metrics rather than just circulation figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and budget production carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Slick color magazines are very expensive, while offset newsletters can be relatively inexpensive. All take time to produce, however. Budget a publication carefully before you commit your organization to its production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get estimates from printers and typesetters, consult with editors in other organizations about production costs, and account for number of people and time needed. Consider lead times and staff commitments before approving production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify lead time and production schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead time for a publication—the time needed to develop article ideas, make assignments to writers and artists, and allow the printer to set type, make up pages, and do the complete printing job—typically is two to three months. The editor must spell out which activities take place, in what order, and with what time separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Gantt charts or similar scheduling tools. Tailor lead times to periodicity (weekly may be ~10 days; annual reports may take a year). Provide milestone timing (example monthly schedule: 90 days story list, 70 first drafts, 60 photography assignments, 50 final drafts/rough dummies, 25 proofreading/comprehensive, 10 mechanicals/final corrections, 0 distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the four basic typographical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Layout means placement of the four basic elements of typographical design: 1. Body type (text). 2. Display type (headlines, titles, 'teasers'). 3. Art (photos, drawings, graphic elements). 4. White space (air, or 'visual freedom').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each page or spread plans for these elements from rough sketches through comprehensive comps to mechanicals. Use layout sheets (light-blue pencil on blue layout forms) because the blue won't photograph in offset; follow layout phases: rough layout (dummy), comprehensive layout ('comp'), mechanical layout (camera-ready paste-up).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow three layout preparation phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Each page or two-page spread goes through three phases of preparation: 1. Rough layout or dummy. 2. Comprehensive layout ('comp'). 3. Mechanical layout—a paste-up into camera-ready layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rough to visualize, the comp to measure exact space for items, and mechanicals for camera-ready production. Decide whether to produce mechanicals in-house or let the printer handle them once comp approved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose number of columns for readability and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: When you first sit down to design the format for your newsletter, the initial decision involves the number of columns per page. A single full-width column of type is difficult to read; two-column allows readability but limits layout variation; three- and four-column formats permit many combinations and visual variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-column for readable type but limited variety; three/four columns for flexibility (one-, two-, multiple-column items), picture sizes, and headline widths. Be aware that narrower columns shrink copy space, increase hyphenation and odd spacing—tradeoffs accepted for flexibility. Consider 'one-and-two' or mixed formats (outside single column + double-width other columns) to add interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use column widths to 'grade' news and vary visual hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-column format allows the editor to 'grade' the news better and to offer greater variety in sizes of type. Editors can use one-column 'mug shots', two-column shots for small groups, and three-column display type or special art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage varying column widths to signal importance and create typographic variety. Stack headlines and pictures in free columns where appropriate to attract attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add white space and simple graphic rules to define style
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t underestimate the ability of such basic graphic elements as cutoff rules and border treatments to create the style and 'feel' of your publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use border treatments, cutoff rules, alternating bold/light rules, and white space strategically to give character to the nameplate and highlight featured articles. Simple graphic devices can be cost-effective styling tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice copyfitting to make text fit assigned space
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Copyfitting’ means developing a counting and estimating scheme for headlines and text. The editor must assure that the edited material precisely fits the assigned space on the layout sheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn systems for estimating type; plan subheadings and line counts; use galley proofs and successive proof stages to track necessary adjustments. Budget for copy shrinkage when moving to multiple-column layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent corporate graphic identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The logo, slogan, and proprietary color selected to represent the organization should appear prominently in every publication’s nameplate. If your organization publishes several publications for special audiences, the family tie should be apparent in typeface and graphic styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure readers can recognize organizational personality and style even if they encounter publications not targeted at them. Announce changes to corporate identity in-house publications first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate story ideas proactively from internal sources
rubrics_metrics.description: All meetings held by the organization are potential 'story sessions.' The editor should meet frequently with department heads and committee chairpersons, take walking tours, monitor bulletin boards, and set up a network of 'stringers' to bring in items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use meetings, interviews, plant tours, department stringers (consider small payments, e.g., $25 per used short article), and reading related publications to localize broader topics. Exchange subscriptions with peer publications and affiliate with professional associations for ideas and workshops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use postpublication critique and planning meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: A postpublication critique, in which the entire PR staff analyzes the effectiveness of the current issue, should generate ideas for the next one. A quarterly planning meeting should be used to generate ideas for the next three or four issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite department heads and outsiders to critiques to strengthen the publication's role and quality. Use critique findings to inform editorial planning and to avoid predictability/rut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a communication objective for photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine a communication objective when you take or choose a photograph. Don’t choose a photo just because it is interesting or artistic; determine whether viewers will understand and retain the intended message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat photographs like other messages: be intentional about the meaning you want to convey. Recognize that photographs rarely change attitudes or behaviors alone, though dramatic photos sometimes can.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider visual complexity relative to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs are more complex than illustrations or graphs—they carry more information. Because photographs are complex they’re effective at getting and holding the attention of low-involvement, passive publics; illustrations/graphs are better for communicating difficult ideas to active, high-involvement audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use photographs to attract attention for general-interest or passive readers; use graphs/illustrations for financial data, research results, or technical information that requires precise, less-ambiguous messages. Example: Science 81 uses photos to gain attention; Scientific American uses graphs/illustrations for application by specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate photographs as part of readership measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate pictures as part of a readership study: ask if people remember seeing a photograph (recognition), what message they think the photograph conveyed (retention), and whether they believe the photograph portrayed a situation accurately (acceptance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If selecting attitude or behavior objectives for photos, apply the same attitude/behavior measures used for text (Chapter 9), but note it's difficult to separate photo effects from accompanying text. Compare media coverage/clippings when releases go with vs. without pictures to assess impact on media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage photographic resources and supply visuals to media
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs supplement written or spoken communication and sometimes carry the entire message. PR people need skills to prepare pictures and illustrations for layouts and for media distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider in-house photo operations, the management of photographic assignments, and the preparation of images (captions, cutlines, croppings). Coordinate with printers for engraving and proofs; use galley proofs and 'blues' to identify printing-quality issues before final plates.
